text: Good afternoon. I am going to call the Land Use Policy Committee meeting to order, and the first thing on the agenda is the acceptance of our minutes from the last meeting, so unless I see any questions or corrections, those will stand as accepted.

We have three presentations today. A lot of them are following up from board matters and information the staff wanted to get. So we're going to get right into Parking Reimagined. Michael, are you going to kick us off? Thank you.

So after Parking Reimagined was adopted by the board in September of 2023, as a follow-on motion, staff was asked to look at accessible parking as questions came up about the supply of accessible parking and what the effect of the new minimum requirements would have on that.

So after that motion was adopted by the board, we started to look at this more specifically and tried to, first of all, see what effect that would have, the changes in the rates would have on accessible parking supply.

So we assessed that there could indeed be a difference associated with that and then set about getting some information together to make a recommendation to the board. So we first made an assessment about, as I said, about accessible parking and the supply circumstance.
We wanted to get some information, some survey data, both field surveys as well as citizen surveys. So in January of this year, we initiated both of those projects.

We started doing field surveys of high-demand uses, such as grocery stores, restaurants, public facilities, and those types of things where we'd expect more demand for parking generally as well as for accessible parking.

As the behavior, I mean, it's human behavior. People are going to shop at Walmart whether you need accessible parking or general parking. So with the field surveys that we took, we found that capacity was generally available for accessible parking. There was, in 92% of the sites that were surveyed during the peak demand times and general demand times, we avoided surveying during a time when we knew that there would be no parking demand, that 92% of the time there was an accessible space available.
And we also, as part of that, were looking to see if there were any sort of violations of accessible parking in the sense that there was no display card in the vehicle or no accessible license plate.

And that we found was very minimal circumstance or probably only about, on average, about 60% of violations over the sites that we surveyed. And we surveyed over 300 time points between January and May 31st.
The other thing that we did was we worked with Human Services to put together a community survey. And that was available, put the survey together, and we made it available online.

And we had that up from March to April 15th. We had a significant amount of feedback on that, not only from respondents to the survey itself, but a lot of comments as well. And we made an effort to ensure that, you know, there was a press release associated with it and it was information was provided to the supervisor's office.

So we did get a very good response. I was very happy with that. And the feedback that we got really kind of reinforced where we were heading with maintaining the supply of accessible parking. Because if you make changes to parking, the accessible parking spaces are based on the number of overall spaces that are provided on the site.

And so with the changes that we made to Parking Reimagined to require less parking, that could conceivably lead to less accessible parking within areas of the county. the non-tiered framework areas, if you recall how we set that up.

There were also concerns expressed in the comments about accessible space design and accessibility concerns associated with parking and accessing buildings. So we're still continuing to look at that as well. One of the things that we are considering is there have been some issues with the hatched areas next to van accessible spaces and people parking on those areas or crowding those areas.

And so there could be some signage or pavement markings that we could put into place that would discourage people parking on those areas. So the recommendations that we have are to increase the accessible parking ratio to compensate for the changes that we made to the baseline parking requirements in the ordinance.
We're proposing generally a 1 to 15 ratio to the 1 to 25 ratio. I know this is all very technical. That is in the current requirement in the Virginia Statewide Building Code.

So we would propose that the county adopt its own ratio into the ordinance. And then, as I said, we're looking at other potential modifications that may require modifications to the public facilities manual.

So just briefly, just to give you a quick comparative of the 1 to 25 versus the 1 to 15, you can see generally in the chart that the thresholds for the 1 to 15 on the right side are more readily achieved.

So, you know, if you have today, an accessible space would be required for anything 25 spaces or less, whereas the new requirement would be 15 spaces or less. And that kind of translates all the way through the 1 to 15 chart.

So I took a look at a particular use. Just to give you a comparative, we have restaurant use for the baseline parking requirement had a fairly significant change. It went from a 1 to 10 or 1 to 15 or 1 to 11 space ratio based on square footage to a 1 to 8 parking ratio.
So you can see on the bar chart that for the 1 to 25 in the pre-parking amendment, you see the blue thresholds.

The gray thresholds would be with the current parking minimum, which in the case of the 10,000 and 15,000 square foot restaurant would be less accessible parking required if you built the minimum amount of parking. And then the 1 to 15 shows that there would be an increase in the 5,000 to 10,000 square foot range for a restaurant if the 1 to 15 ratio was adopted.

So we've accomplished most of these steps presenting today to you. Our hope would be that the board supports this initiative and wants staff to move forward with it. And with that, we would expect that it would be another six months or so to get back to the board with an ordinance, a proposed ordinance amendment for consideration.

And with that, my presentation is concluded. Thank you. You know, I think this is a good example of when the community comes to us with a concern and staff can go do the research. I did go through the nip again and to read the comments from people about where their concerns were.

And I'm here today to give an update on a zoning ordinance amendment related to the use contractors' offices and shops. and the topic of construction vehicles and the regulation for construction vehicles and the ordinance so just some background here looking at uh the timeline related to this amendment this this started as supervisor smith noted um following uh the adoption of z mod and uh staff at the time was asked to do research on this project and determine uh if there was flexibility

needed in the ordinance relating to uh contractors offices and jobs and construction vehicles And so my colleagues, Sarah Morgan, at the time then held community outreach meetings to determine kind of the need here and some of the issues that were seen within the community about contractors' offices and shops and the regulation of construction vehicles.

And this then was taken to, in May of 2022, to a land use policy committee meeting where it was formally made into a zoning ordinance amendment project. And since such time, we've kind of had a re-kickstart on this project. Our office was working on things like landscaping and screening and parking reimagined.

And as such, we kick-started this amendment in the beginning of this year and held multiple community outreach meetings, meetings with some district-specific groups related to kind of our proposal and trying to understand, you know, what is needed here and the issues that are impacting contractors' offices within the county.

And as you can see on the screen, we went to the Land Use Policy Review Committee or Land Use Process Review Committee in May of this year and are hoping to have a final product authorized likely in September of this year and then hopefully going to board and planning commission hearings before the end of the year.

So just to talk a little bit about contractors' offices and shops, this use is broad. It covers your HVAC technicians, plumbers, electricians, roofing companies, and it also includes landscape companies.

And so it includes groups that might be doing landscaping, hardscaping, and it also includes your tree companies, your arborists. And it's currently permitted by right in the C8, I3, I4, I5, and I6 districts and in the PTC districts when shown in a final development plan.

the existing kind of provisions um and limitations on the use specifically in the c8 i3 and i4 district um it was part of the main conversation that we had with the community um the use is limited to 500 square feet of outdoor storage currently in the c8 i3 and i4 districts and that storage must be screened from view and then another major part of this is that the parking of construction equipment machinery dump trucks things of that nature is not permitted by right

in the c8 i3 and i4 districts and what i'll note here is that during outreach we heard from contractors across the board a desire to be able to serve their community better and that was something that was pampered by a lack of areas for them to establish these contractors were looking for areas to go to. And currently, they were finding that, you know, there's just really not a whole lot of industrial land that they can establish in. And there was also a desire for a need for objective definitions and clear regulations. So currently we have in the ordinance, we don't

have a specific definition for construction vehicles and equipment. We have some provisions that talk to what it could be and a desire to see these objective regulations established within the ordinance. And when I talk about kind of the overall trend of industrial, I mean, currently we have approximately 8,000 acres zoned to industrial districts within the county and approximately 3,700 acres planned for industrial. So these are uses that are our contractors that are servicing our homes in time of emergency when we have a water leak at night, as well as people who are coming out to just service our homes and businesses at other times. So

definitely a very important use within the county. So some of the things we're looking at and the potential changes is addressing the issue of defining construction vehicles. And so during our outreach, we asked community members kind of their general feeling towards certain pieces of equipment. We showed them photos during outreach meetings and talked about these types of pieces of equipment and where they could be kept. And this kind of helped us to form a possible, two possible definitions for light and heavy vehicles and equipment.

And I'll note that the light vehicles and equipment are essentially vehicles that are commonly seen in association with contractors' offices and shops, and the heavy vehicles are those that we consider now construction vehicles. It's your dump trucks, your tow trucks, your larger vehicles, things that most people were not comfortable seeing in somewhere like a C8 district.

And so that leads me to kind of where another place we're going with this proposed amendment is allowing for both light and heavy vehicles to be kept in the I-3 and the I-4 district. And so currently, you cannot keep construction-style equipment in the industrial 3 and industrial 4 districts.

This was a major concern we heard from contractors of where. A lot of our contractors may actually not need a physical office space. They're looking for a place to keep their equipment and without having the I-3 and the four district to do that and they're limited to i-5 and i-6 storage yards to keep their equipment or if they have an established contractor's office and shop and then further looking to preserve the intent of the ordinance which is to prohibit construction vehicles and equipment and the heavy vehicles and equipment in the c8 highway commercial district and less approved through a special exception and the example i'll give with this is that a good example is a tree company a tree company a lot of times has a vehicle that might be larger than what normally would be allowed they

They may not have a bunch of these vehicles. They may have two, three, four of these vehicles. And we are looking at the possibility of allowing for a special exception to process to keep a specific amount of vehicles and type of vehicles on the property. And when we talk about the definitions, we talk about the proposals for these things like light vehicles and equipment.

Again, these are vehicles that we commonly see in association with the use and oftentimes are the subject of violations. We're looking to add objective standards that deal with things like length, height, Gross vehicle weight, number of axles, and then rated operating capacity for equipment.

And I'll speak to gross vehicle weight rating. This is a standard that all vehicles have. The proposal of 16,001 pounds is based on both our county code as well on federal highway classifications of vehicles. It's the class 5 vehicle rating.

And once you get above that, you start to get into things like dump trucks. And we know we have previously in the ordinance determined those are considered construction vehicles and would like to keep it kind of around that range of that 16,000 pounds or less, you know, for the definition here. And then further, when it comes to things like height, length, these are the things that we've seen in other parts of the ordinance.

We see it for use standards, for uses such as a goods distribution hub, and this kind of style of breakdown is seen throughout the ordinance. And then lastly, rated operating capacity. This is not just equipment. they're not just vehicles this is equipment so a contractor might have a bobcat a skid steer a ditch witch something of those in that nature and we're looking at adding this rated operating capacity which is an industry standard for pieces of equipment that are made to pick things up the expectation is that this equipment will be stored within screened areas but but a possibility to keep these things within a c8 district so when we talk about heavy vehicles

our heavy vehicles are again our traditional construction vehicles our dump trucks solid waste collection vehicles. And what I'll note is that with the light and heavy standards, and I should have noted this in the previous slide, is that if a vehicle meets or exceeds any one of the light standards, it would be considered a heavy vehicle.

And at that time, then subject to this. And heavy vehicles and equipment, again, we're looking to not permit buy right in the C8 district and then change the ordinance, hopefully, to look at keeping of these vehicles in the I-3 and the I-4 district to allow more space to keep them in the county.

And so potential changes as it relates to outdoor storage associated with the use. So we're looking at the possibility of increasing outdoor storage by right in the C8, I3, and I4 district. The white paper that I wrote in relation to this presentation talks about 1,000 square feet of outdoor storage for a C8 district.

And this is, we'll touch on in another slide, kind of the overall, you know, footprint of what that looks like and what currently is permitted. But looking to also establish a special exception process, establish an SE process in the C8 district to allow for increased outdoor storage.

So one of the things that we heard during community outreach on this was support for contractors, support for knowing that we need some of these uses in these areas, but also wanting to establish regulations that protect the commercial nature of these properties and also take into consideration the effect they can have on residential abutting properties.

And then in the I-3 and the I-4 districts, we are looking at the possibility of allowing for storage yards as a principal use. Storage yards currently are not permitted in the I-3 and the I-4 district by right. It's only through special exception and only when in conjunction with a self-storage use. And so this would be a limited storage use that would be allowed, limited to 10,000 square feet by right.

It would need to be screened in with something like a six-foot tall fence. And then also establishing a special exception process to permit larger storage yards over that 10,000 square feet in the I-3 and the I-4 district. And then lastly, the outdoor storage related to these uses would not be permitted in any front yards.

So as mentioned, we talk about overall square footage. The left-hand side of the screen shows 10,000 square feet. It's pieces of equipment that are needed for the use. And we feel that, you know, allowing for an increased outdoor storage of some by right and then the special exception option really does allow for flexibility for these contractors to establish and have an area to work in.

Now, I will say the increased outdoor storage is subject to site plan approval that would be required to get site plan approval for anything over 500 square feet. And we're also, as part of this amendment, looking at regulations related to approval of that outdoor storage.

Currently, there is no limit of the amount of outdoor storage that can be permitted by site plan. And this amendment looks to kind of put guardrails on the amount that can be permitted by right and the amount that's permitted through special exception.
